children.topic: I. Indications for Surgery
Symptomatic gallstones = primary indication for elective cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic (silent) gallstones: generally NOT indicated, except:
Porcelain (calcified) gallbladder — high risk of adenocarcinoma (especially scattered calcifications)
Diabetic and immunosuppressed patients — high risk of gangrene or emphysematous cholecystitis
Young/fit patients — to prevent long-term complications
Gallbladder polyps: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for any polyp ≥ 6 mm due to malignant risk
Infections and inflammatory states:
Acute cholecystitis — early urgent surgery preferred
Chronic calculous and non-calculous cholecystitis (e.g., chronic Typhoid carriers)
Mucocele and empyema — high risk of perforation, urgent intervention needed
Congenital anomalies (e.g., septated gallbladder)
Trauma (ruptured or torsed gallbladder)
Neoplastic (operable carcinoma of gallbladder)
II. Laparoscopic vs. Open Approach
Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (LC) — Gold Standard
Advantages: magnified visualization, less tissue trauma, less postoperative pain, reduced dynamic ileus, lower wound infection/dehiscence rates, shorter hospital stay, faster return to activities
Limitations: problematic hand-eye coordination, complex/longer instrumentation, lack of tactile feedback, more challenging homeostasis
Contraindications — Absolute: inability to undergo general anesthesia, direct patient refusal

Contraindications — Relative: lack of surgical training, advanced cancer, previous extensive upper abdominal surgery (dense adhesions), severe cardiopulmonary disease, morbid obesity, portal hypertension, coagulopathy
Open Cholecystectomy — standard fallback approach
Indicated when laparoscopic visualization is severely compromised
Used when converted intraoperatively due to dense fibrous adhesions or uncontrollable bleeding
III. Laparoscopic Principles & Pneumoperitoneum
Creating pneumoperitoneum:
Gas of choice: CO2 introduced via a Veress needle
Volume and pressure: 3-4 liters of CO2 until intra-abdominal pressure reaches 12-14 mmHg
Why CO2: highly soluble (minimizes embolization risk), non-combustible, compatible with electrocoagulation
Hazards: high pressure (> 20 mmHg) reduces venous return (CVP decreases), can cause hypercarbia, cardiac arrhythmias, CO2 gas embolism
Surgical problems and safety:
Access injuries: Veress needle or trocar can perforate major retroperitoneal blood vessels or hollow viscera (stomach, bowel, bladder)
Electrical/thermal injuries: monopolar electrosurgery can cause inadvertent bowel or biliary tract burns via direct touch, insulation breakdown, or capacitive coupling
Thermal injuries typically manifest 3-7 days postoperatively with delayed peritonitis
IV. Surgical Complications
CBD Injury (1-7%): most feared and devastating specific complication
Risk factors: male patients, operations for acute cholecystitis (severe inflammation and edema)
Mechanism: CBD mistaken for the cystic duct, inadvertently clipped and divided
Consequences: biliary leaks, postoperative bile peritonitis, chronic strictures causing obstructive jaundice, recurrent cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis
Vascular injury: right hepatic artery at high risk, especially with anomalous course (Caterpillar hump / Moynihan's hump) — loops in front of CBD
Bowel injury: perforation of duodenum or hepatic flexure of colon
Postoperative bile leakage: from unrecognized duct of Luschka, slipped clip on cystic duct stump, or major duct injury
Missed CBD stone: a retained stone left behind in the biliary tree
V. Post-Op Workup (Bile Leaks & HIDA)
Clinical presentation: within first week after cholecystectomy — persistent abdominal pain, distention, low-grade fever, anorexia — suspect biloma or postoperative bleeding
Step 1 — Imaging (CT or U/S): look for fluid collection; if large, drain percutaneously
Step 2 — Check the fluid: if bilious, bile leak is confirmed
Step 3 — HIDA scan (cholescintigraphy): determines origin and severity of leak
Cystic duct stump leak: tracer extravasates into RUQ BUT tracer STILL seen flowing into duodenum/small bowel (main ductal integrity confirmed)
Cause: surgical clip slipped off the cystic duct stump
Management: ERCP with stenting of the sphincter of Oddi — lowers biliary tree pressure, creates path of least resistance, allows stump to seal
Major ductal injury (CBD/CHD transection): tracer extravasation into peritoneum WITHOUT any tracer entering small bowel
Management: surgical reconstruction via Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (jejunum anastomosed to proximal healthy bile duct)
VI. Post-Cholecystectomy Syndrome (PCS)
Definition: recurrent or persistent RUQ/epigastric symptoms continuing weeks or months after cholecystectomy
Etiologies:
Residual/retained stone in CBD — can trigger biliary obstruction, acute ascending cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis
Long cystic duct stump — can harbor a retained stone or allow new stone formation
Sphincter of Oddi Dysfunction (SOD) — rare functional disorder (stenosis or dyskinesia)
Episodic RUQ pain classically precipitated/worsened by opioids (e.g., morphine) due to opioid-induced sphincter spasm
Diagnosed with manometry; treated with ERCP sphincterotomy
Missed non-biliary pathology: gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, or chronic pancreatitis that was present before surgery and mistaken for gallstone pain
VII. Post-Operative Care & Expected Sequelae
Early recovery (LC): mobilization next morning, oral intake after 6 hours, discharge within 24 hours
Expected post-op symptoms:
Nausea
Shoulder pain — referred pain from phrenic nerve irritation by retained subdiaphragmatic CO2 gas
Mild abdominal pain
Time to normal activity: full recovery and return to work typically within 10 days
